_about: Plain-language summaries written for this website from each paper's abstract. Not part of the proceedings; shown in green and labelled as added.

reward-free-continual-adaptation-resilie.tldr: A robot in space can break in ways nobody planned for, and there is usually no one around to score how well it is doing afterwards. The authors teach a robot an internal model of its world in simulation, then let it update only how it thinks its body moves after damage, so it can relearn to act without any new reward signal. They test this on simulated rovers, orbital craft and assembly arms with severe failures.

comparative-performance-analysis-classic.tldr: To service a satellite in orbit, a robot first has to find the ring where the satellite was attached to its rocket. This paper compares a classical image-processing detector with a small neural network (YOLOv8n). The neural network copes better with changing light; the classical method needs far less computing power.

astropie-53-towards-understanding-failur.tldr: Software that detects people and their body poses works well on Earth, but nobody had measured how it does on astronauts. The authors build a small annotated set of 53 astronaut videos and test current detectors on it. Spacesuits, unusual body orientations, low contrast and occlusion all cause large drops in accuracy.

data-centric-preprocessing-gnss-based-or.tldr: Working out a satellite's orbit from GPS-type measurements goes wrong when the measurements contain errors. This paper builds a cleaning pipeline that first checks whether the data look structured enough before applying stronger cleaning steps, guided by a small classifier. It removes the obvious outliers, also catches subtler inconsistent points, and gives a more stable orbit estimate.

high-fidelity-low-earth-orbit-determinat.tldr: Classical orbit estimation needs a good first guess of where the satellite is. This paper uses a physics-informed extreme learning machine, a fast network trained to fit the measurements while obeying the equations of motion, with a detailed model of the forces in low orbit. On a stretch of the International Space Station's orbit it reconstructs the trajectory accurately without needing that first guess.

offline-approximate-value-iteration-rein.tldr: Building a satellite constellation means deciding, launch after launch, where to put satellites while some launches or satellites fail. The authors frame this as a sequential decision problem and solve it with an approximate reinforcement-learning method made tractable by simple function approximation and pruning. The resulting policies deploy constellations faster and more cheaply than a planning baseline.

identification-rare-weak-signals-machine.tldr: Finding exoplanets in TESS telescope data means sifting through huge numbers of light curves. The authors train an ensemble of three neural networks on over a million volunteer-labelled light curves to imitate and prioritise human judgement. The models recovered as many known objects as the volunteers, and the targets they disagreed on turned out to be volunteer false alarms.

metallicity-conditioned-transformer-base.tldr: Knowing which stars are likely to host certain planets helps telescopes spend observing time well. The authors extend a transformer that generates whole planetary systems so it also takes the star's metal content into account. Hiding planets in known systems and asking the model to predict them shows that using metallicity gives tighter, more useful predictions.

faithful-neural-embeddings-3d-exoplanet-.tldr: 3D climate simulations of exoplanet atmospheres are slow. This paper compresses whole temperature profiles into a small set of numbers using autoencoders, as a first step towards a fast emulator that predicts complete profiles instead of single points. The compressed representation reproduces the profiles faithfully.

onboard-predictive-fault-management-sera.tldr: Spacecraft normally react to faults only after a limit is crossed. This paper describes an experiment for the SeRANIS mission that forecasts telemetry over short, medium and long horizons on an AI-capable onboard computer, to spot trouble before limits are hit. It compares forecasting and anomaly-detection methods before flight, including how much computing they need.

comparative-study-reconstruction-based-d.tldr: One way to spot anomalies in spacecraft telemetry is to train a model to reconstruct normal data and flag what it cannot reconstruct. The authors compare four such deep-learning models on public benchmarks and real satellite data under identical settings. Transformer-based models do best, with Anomaly-Transformer giving the best balance of precision and recall.

foundation-model-assessment-state-health.tldr: Predicting how a satellite battery wears out is hard because there is little data from real missions. The authors test a time-series foundation model (Chronos-2), pre-trained on huge amounts of unrelated data, on NASA battery tests without retraining it on batteries. It predicts battery health accurately and also gives confidence bands.

mpc-underactuated-spacecraft-control-lya.tldr: Pointing a spacecraft that cannot push on every axis is difficult, especially when its mass properties are not exactly known. The authors combine a model-predictive controller with a physics-informed neural network that estimates unmodelled disturbances, plus a safety supervisor that switches the network's correction off when it cannot be trusted. In simulation this reduces pointing errors while keeping the original controller's stability.

adversarial-reinforcement-learning-robus.tldr: Landing controllers trained with random disturbances can miss the correlated disturbances real missions face. Here a second learning agent acts as an adversary, deliberately pushing the lander in the hardest physically allowed ways, and the two are trained against each other. Early results show the adversary finds weaknesses that random testing misses.

learning-cross-view-correspondences-geo-.tldr: A rover on the Moon has no GPS, so it must work out where it is by comparing what it sees with maps taken from orbit. The authors build a benchmark of over 10,000 rendered lunar surface panoramas paired with matching overhead images. A modern learning-based matching method trained on it localises successfully, suggesting a vision-based alternative to satellite navigation.

geometry-learned-representations-event-b.tldr: This paper looks inside a neural network that estimates a spacecraft's motion from an event camera, inertial sensors and range measurements. The network's internal representation turns out to be organised along the actual motion variables, and its attention shifts between sensors depending on how reliable they are. This links the learned approach to classical estimation theory.

deploying-neural-networks-fpgas-earth-ob.tldr: Satellites can save downlink bandwidth by deciding onboard which images matter, but the neural networks have to fit low-power hardware. The authors extend two toolchains (hls4ml and CGRA4ML) so image-segmentation networks run on the European NanoXplore NG-ULTRA chip. They demonstrate it by detecting plastic pollution in the oceans.

assessing-impact-off-nadir-image-acquisi.tldr: Tilting a satellite to image sideways lets it revisit places more often, but could make onboard ship detection worse. Using 38 CogniSAT-6 scenes taken at angles up to 45 degrees, the authors find no significant effect of viewing angle on a ship-segmentation model. What matters most is the contrast between ship and water.

resource-efficient-super-resolution-mult.tldr: This paper sharpens Sentinel-2 imagery four times in each direction (red, green, blue and near-infrared) with a small transformer model meant to run onboard. With only 792,000 parameters it keeps colours more faithful than the previous best method at about a third of the computing cost.

towards-robust-efficient-multispectral-c.tldr: Models that detect changes between satellite images can fail when lighting, calibration or optics differ between acquisitions. The authors propose a training trick (HCAT) that makes each pixel's decision more stable under such physically realistic disturbances, without adding any cost at run time. It clearly improves robustness across three model sizes and on a larger second dataset.

memetic-co-design-2d-locomotion-at-varia.tldr: How should a robot be shaped to walk on a world with different gravity? The authors evolve 2D soft-robot bodies while fine-tuning their movement with gradient-based optimisation. Running this at several gravity levels shows the robots switching between distinct ways of moving as gravity changes.

ai-enhanced-spatial-reconstruction-thin-.tldr: Small radiation monitors for space weather could also tell where a charged particle hit a detector tile, if that position can be reconstructed from a few light sensors. In detailed simulations, machine-learning models cut the typical position error from about 2 cm with the standard method to under 0.6 cm.

breccia-basalt-classification-thin-secti.tldr: Future Moon astronauts could use help choosing which rocks to bring back. Using microscope images of thin slices of Apollo rock samples, the authors pre-train a network with contrastive learning and then teach it to tell two rock types apart. It is right about 94% of the time per image and 99% per sample.

semhopqa-automated-pipeline-generating-q.tldr: To test AI assistants that answer questions from spacecraft documentation, you need good question-and-answer test sets. SemHopQA builds them automatically by turning the documents into a knowledge graph and walking through it to create questions. Compared with a popular chunk-based generator it produces fewer questions, but far more of them are actually answerable.

multi-agent-work-flow-automated-mbse-mod.tldr: Turning written requirements into formal system models is slow manual work in spacecraft engineering. The authors split the job between three cooperating large-language-model agents that analyse the text, generate the model file and check it. The files they produce load into MagicDraw far more reliably than those from a single prompt.

analysis-space-research-through-neural-t.tldr: The authors map three decades of space-related papers on arXiv with neural topic models helped by large language models. The analysis shows which research themes grew, such as multimodal and self-supervised methods, and how methods changed within popular topics. The result is a guide for navigating a fast-growing literature.

robust-flood-extent-mapping-gated-fusion.tldr: Flood maps from satellites usually need radar and optical images taken at the same time, which is rarely available. This model always uses one radar image of the flood and adds whatever else exists, such as optical images or images from before the flood, weighting each with a learned gate. It uses the extra data when present and still works when it is missing.

tenka-physics-guided-multimodal-deep-lea.tldr: Weather satellites see bright flashes from meteors burning up, but lightning causes far more flashes. TENKA combines images, flash timing sequences and physics-based features to tell the two apart. It is very accurate on a balanced test set and produces far fewer false alarms than purely data-driven models under realistic conditions.

methane-detection-board-satellites-unort.tldr: Detecting methane leaks from orbit usually requires ground processing to correct image geometry first. The authors train models directly on uncorrected hyperspectral images, which could run onboard. These come close to models trained on corrected images and far outperform the standard matched-filter method. Data and code are public.

floodcatch-physics-guided-machine-learni.tldr: Radar satellites see through clouds but pass over a flood only every few days. FloodCatch fills in flood maps for the days in between by combining radar-based flood detection with gap-filling that respects physical constraints. The reconstructed floods evolve more smoothly and plausibly than with purely data-driven gap-filling.

fun-q1-scouring-first-euclid-data-astrop.tldr: The authors searched all 30 million sources in the first Euclid data release for unusual objects, using an active-learning tool that improves with each round of human feedback. Starting from 35 known oddities, they found 8,547 candidates, 95% of which had not been described before. The search covered the full dataset in two to three days.

improving-faint-object-detection-space-s.tldr: Faint satellites far from Earth are hard to spot against bright, uneven sky backgrounds full of stars. This pipeline masks the stars with a small network and fills in the background with a variational autoencoder, so the remaining image highlights moving objects. On real telescope data this makes faint targets much easier to detect.

developing-digital-twin-magao-x-telemetr.tldr: Imaging planets next to bright stars is limited by leftover starlight that changes with tiny optical errors. The authors use wavefront-sensor telemetry and a differentiable digital twin of the MagAO-X instrument to predict that leftover starlight and subtract it. In simulation the cleaned images are limited only by photon noise.

traceable-spectral-inference-influence-f.tldr: For the Ariel exoplanet mission there will be no ground truth to check predictions against. This paper traces each prediction back to the training examples that most influenced it, and turns that into an estimate of how wrong a prediction might be. On simulated spectra the error estimate tracks real errors well.

leveraging-parallel-computing-visual-onb.tldr: Earth-observation cameras could also help a satellite know how it is oriented. The authors match features between consecutive Earth images to measure how the satellite has rotated, and run this on space-qualified GPU hardware (GPU@SAT). They report accuracy and run time on that hardware.

prior-knowledge-informed-centroiding-cnn.tldr: For optical navigation, a spacecraft must find the true centre of an irregular, partly shadowed asteroid or moon in an image. This network combines image features with known physical cues and predicts a correction to the brightness centre. It gives the smallest errors on all tested bodies, including ones it never saw in training, and runs in under 55 ms on a small embedded GPU.

ai-driven-framework-automated-identifica.tldr: Radio telescopes like LOFAR record many solar radio bursts that are slow to catalogue by hand. The authors pre-train a model on large amounts of unlabelled LOFAR data with self-supervised learning before training it on a few labelled examples. This makes it possible to detect and classify several burst types automatically, including rare ones.

agile-earth-observation-satellite-schedu.tldr: An agile imaging satellite must constantly decide what to photograph and when to send data down. Here a reinforcement-learning agent proposes edits to a plan made on the ground, and a rule-based routine makes sure every edit is feasible. A transformer-based agent earns more reward and downlinks more than simpler agents, at the cost of changing the plan more often.

improving-board-shape-models-sun-sensors.tldr: A small spacecraft orbiting an asteroid can learn its shape just from when the Sun disappears and reappears behind it, using cheap Sun sensors. The method refines the asteroid's outline from these eclipse events and builds a 3D neural shape model from it. In simulations of asteroid Eros it clearly improves the shape estimate.

identification-gravitational-constant-sa.tldr: Can a neural model recover a physical constant from real satellite orbits? The authors split the equations of motion into known gravity, with the gravitational constant left free, plus a neural network for unknown forces. The constant is recovered to within 0.02% even from guesses that are 150% off, but with worse starting guesses the network absorbs the error instead.

second-order-gradient-informed-spacecraf.tldr: Neural networks can learn spacecraft guidance from optimal trajectories. The authors add training terms derived from second-order relations of optimal control theory, which enforce physical consistency without extra expensive labels. On an Earth-to-Venus low-thrust transfer this gives more accurate and more robust guidance.

learning-based-reconstruction-space-resi.tldr: The authors reconstruct the 3D shape and appearance of an object in orbit from images taken during a single fly-around, using neural radiance fields. Keeping shape and appearance separate stops changing sunlight from being mistaken for structure.

enhancing-ai-trustworthiness-rover-navig.tldr: A Mars rover should know when its terrain classifier is unsure. This work adds calibrated uncertainty to a terrain-segmentation network, with statistical guarantees, and turns it into a risk map for every pixel. A path planner then uses the map to choose safer routes.

launcher-trajectory-criticality-predicti.tldr: A rocket's autonomous flight-safety system must decide quickly whether a flight is going wrong. The authors train recurrent neural networks on simulated launcher flights to predict trajectory failures from navigation data. All models are highly accurate, and their speed is tested on an embedded AMD Kria board.

structure-aware-unsupervised-anomaly-det.tldr: Most telemetry anomaly detectors need labelled past anomalies or a long warm-up. This framework starts flagging anomalies from the second month of a mission without any labels, retraining monthly and choosing alarm thresholds statistically. It performs well on two missions of the ESA anomaly benchmark.

exploring-trade-off-between-structured-p.tldr: Radiation in space can flip single bits in a neural network's memory. Making a network narrower (pruning) makes each run more fragile, but each run is also shorter, so there is less time for a bit flip to happen. The experiments show these effects roughly cancel, so pruning saves energy and time without reducing overall reliability.

physics-informed-convlstm-networks-trans.tldr: Predicting how a spacecraft circuit board heats up normally needs a slow solver. A neural network that is also penalised for breaking energy balance needs far less training data: with 50 examples, its error drops from about 8 K to 0.3 K compared with the same network without physics. With 200 or more examples, worst-case errors stay within the usual 5 K margin.

incremental-online-learning-european-spa.tldr: Satellite telemetry changes over the years, so anomaly detectors trained once can fall out of date. The authors adapt two streaming methods to keep learning during operation on the ESA anomaly benchmark. Learning online clearly improves the benchmark's main score compared with static training.

marker-free-computer-vision-driven-auton.tldr: This system lets a robot arm dock two standard space interfaces using only two greyscale cameras, without visual markers. A network trained on 20,000 images estimates the relative position to within about 8 mm, and to about 5 mm close to docking. It ran autonomous dockings at about 30 frames per second, even with clutter and moving targets.

detecting-lunar-craters-at-scale.tldr: Automatic crater detectors struggle with tiny craters, rough terrain and changing light. The authors build on the OWLv2 detector with a multi-scale approach that processes full Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images and finds craters of many sizes.

hardware-aware-comparison-keypoint-vs-en.tldr: Two ways to estimate another spacecraft's position and orientation from images are compared on real space-grade FPGA hardware. Keypoint-based models are about half as wrong as end-to-end models but run 1.6 to 10 times slower. The study also shows that parameter count and FLOPs are poor predictors of actual run time.

vstb-camera-loop-testbed-space-vision-ai.tldr: To test space-vision AI with real camera effects but without physical mock-ups, VSTB shows rendered space scenes on a display that a real camera films inside a closed box. It supports data generation, model testing and closed-loop simulation at 10 frames per second, and the camera's subtle effects measurably change neural-network results.

geoai-practice-evaluating-unified-open-s.tldr: Geospatial machine learning in Python is spread over many separate libraries. The authors compare the GeoAI library with TorchGeo and TerraTorch on land-cover classification and building-footprint extraction under identical conditions. GeoAI needs over 80% less code and fewer separate tools.

aligning-human-oversight-aerospace-cross.tldr: The EU AI Act requires human oversight of high-risk AI, but it is unclear what that means in day-to-day space operations. Drawing on the AI Act, aviation guidance, ESA and NASA practice and human-factors research, the authors propose a catalogue of concrete oversight actions and the evidence that shows they were done. A collision-avoidance example shows how to apply it.

planet-detection-protoplanetary-disks-sy.tldr: A young planet hidden in a disk of gas around a star slightly breaks the disk's symmetry. The authors feed measures of these symmetry breaks to their models and compare this with networks built to respect symmetry. The best combination classifies 94.6% of simulated disks correctly as having a planet or not.

quantum-inspired-convolutional-networks-.tldr: Detailed land-cover maps are scarce, but coarse ones are not. This network, using quantum-inspired convolution blocks, combines radar and optical satellite images and is guided only by coarse land-cover labels to produce detailed labels. The results are more spatially coherent than classical baselines.

reinforcement-learning-co-planar-multi-t.tldr: A solar-sail spacecraft preparing for debris removal should visit several orbits in the fastest possible order. With a quick semi-analytical estimate of transfer times, the authors train reinforcement-learning agents to choose the order. The agents find optimal or near-optimal sequences, matching established optimisation methods.

covariance-estimation-orbit-determinatio.tldr: Orbit estimates need error bars to be useful. This paper shows how to compute time-varying position uncertainties for orbits estimated with physics-informed extreme learning machines. Compared with a classical method and Monte Carlo tests, the uncertainties are of the right size, but drift systematically along the orbit.

syndaq-synthetic-data-generation-qualifi.tldr: When real data are scarce or sensitive, synthetic data can help train models. The authors try methods to generate synthetic documentation text, telemetry and telescope images for space operations, and share what worked and what they learned.

ai-based-classification-simulated-cosmic.tldr: A commercial FPGA can double as a radiation detector by watching its own memory for flipped bits, but bursts of hits overflow its telemetry. A tiny neural network on the chip groups related bit flips so less data needs to be sent. Unlike the existing method, it works without calibrating for the chip's memory layout.

space-kbp-dataset-end-end-knowledge-base.tldr: SPACE-KBP is a new dataset for turning space-mission descriptions into structured knowledge that follows the ESA mission ontology. Small language models fine-tuned on it match or beat larger ones, and no longer need the ontology spelled out in the prompt.

stellar-apps-software-execution-platform.tldr: Stellar Apps is a software platform for safely running third-party applications, including AI, on spacecraft computers. It isolates applications from each other, shares the computer between several users, supports real-time work and AI accelerators, and allows updates in orbit.

reinforcement-learning-optimized-sensor-.tldr: Estimating evaporation over large areas needs measurements from well-chosen places. The authors use reinforcement learning to choose a small set of representative locations, using about 2% of all grid points, and train a 3D neural network surrogate on them. Across Italian river basins this predicts better than baseline methods.

uncertainty-aware-surrogate-modeling-thr.tldr: Some rocket nozzles can steer thrust by throttling their two sides differently, but simulating this is expensive. Three fast surrogate models trained on flow simulations predict the thrust and its angle with error bars. Gaussian process regression is the most accurate and gives well-calibrated uncertainty.

reducing-false-positives-wide-field-astr.tldr: Satellites crossing telescope images leave streaks that reveal their orbits, but an existing streak detector raised too many false alarms on archive data. A small extra classifier removes 96% of the false alarms while keeping 97% of real streaks. This makes it practical to process the whole telescope archive.

towards-automated-grain-size-analysis-ex.tldr: Grain size tells geologists a lot about sediments, which matters for ExoMars' search for preserved organic material. The authors review methods and adapt a deep-learning segmentation tool to measure grain sizes in images like those from the rover's cameras. They show first results on 21 Antarctic analogue samples.

ground-orbit-enabling-real-time-board-an.tldr: ATHMoS has detected unusual spacecraft behaviour on the ground at the German Space Operations Center since 2022. This paper adapts it to run onboard in real time with limited computing power. Detecting anomalies onboard means operators no longer have to wait for the next ground contact to learn about them.

online-learning-dynamic-constellation-to.tldr: Satellites in a network keep moving, so which ones should link to each other keeps changing. The authors treat the choice of links as an online learning problem that makes no assumptions about orbital planes. It matches state-of-the-art offline methods and allows trading computation per step against how fast it converges.

transformer-attention-as-domain-clusteri.tldr: Huge sky surveys need ways to group similar objects automatically. Comparing a CNN with two vision transformers on Euclid images, the authors find transformer embeddings often separate meaningful groups clearly, such as galaxy types or stars versus galaxies. This could be used to filter survey data before expensive analysis.

cross-task-analysis-post-training-quanti.tldr: Shrinking neural networks to 8-bit integers saves memory and power onboard, but may cost accuracy. On classification, object detection and segmentation of Earth-observation data, classification and segmentation lose little. Object detection is much more sensitive.

data-driven-framework-space-tailored-sta.tldr: This work estimates the health of a satellite's lithium-ion battery with a machine-learning model, tests it under different operating conditions, and compresses it to run on small microcontrollers. It also proposes a battery-management system architecture to host it.

differentiable-mascons-spatialmass-joint.tldr: Modelling the gravity around an irregular asteroid often uses many point masses on a fixed grid. Here both the masses and their positions are optimised, and points are moved to where errors are largest. On a challenging asteroid benchmark this cuts far-field errors by up to ten times compared with fixed grids and neural baselines.

accelerating-integer-quantized-ai-relate.tldr: The authors add special instructions (SWAR) to the GR765 space-grade processor that do several small integer calculations at once, as needed for quantised neural networks. With compiler and software support, typical space workloads, including machine learning, run noticeably faster.

manusat-onboard-edge-ai-health-monitorin.tldr: Early bearing damage in a satellite's attitude-control gyroscopes shows up as high-frequency vibration that is too much data to send to the ground. MANUSAT analyses the vibrations onboard with autoencoders on an FPGA. It separates healthy from severely faulty bearings perfectly and runs in 70 ms.

early-detection-satellite-telemetry-data.tldr: Instead of flagging anomalies once they appear, SatAnomHD predicts future telemetry and warns seconds to minutes in advance. It uses hyperdimensional computing, a lightweight learning method suited to small satellites. It matches the precision of the best existing method while running up to 60 times faster and using far less energy.

boosting-sentinel-2-crop-disease-classif.tldr: Using Sentinel-2 images from a Kaggle challenge, the authors classify four crop diseases and compare a CNN with a transformer backbone, with and without self-supervised pre-training. Pre-training helps, especially for the transformer, and explanation maps show the models focus on relevant fields and spectral bands.

rapid-prediction-exoplanetary-cloud-prop.tldr: Computing clouds in exoplanet atmospheres requires solving expensive equations at every point of a climate model. A neural network that works through a compressed representation learned by an autoencoder predicts cloud properties quickly. It is accurate for cooler planets; errors grow for hotter ones, where cloud formation is more complex.

automated-satellite-conjunction-manageme.tldr: When two objects in orbit approach each other, operators receive a series of conjunction messages. This transformer model predicts the next message and how uncertain that prediction is. It is more accurate than recurrent networks on two datasets while using fewer parameters.
